{{Short description|Mathematical condition}}
In mathematics, the '''Poincaré lemma''' gives a sufficient condition for a [[closed differential form]] to be exact (while an exact form is necessarily closed). Precisely, it states that every closed ''p''-form on an open ball in '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> is exact for ''p'' with {{nowrap|1 ≤ ''p'' ≤ ''n''}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Warner|1983|pages=155–156}}</ref> The lemma was introduced by [[Henri Poincaré]] in 1886.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s40329-013-0003-3 |title=Henri Poincaré and algebraic geometry |year=2013 |last1=Ciliberto |first1=Ciro |journal=Lettera Matematica |volume=1 |issue=1–2 |pages=23–31 |s2cid=122614329 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Poincaré |first1=H. |title=Sur les résidus des intégrales doubles |journal=Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des sciences |year=1886 |volume=102 |pages=202–204 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k3058f/f202.item}}</ref>

== Informal discussion ==

Especially in [[calculus]], the Poincaré lemma also says that every closed 1-form on a [[simply connected space|simply connected]] [[Open set|open subset]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is exact.

In simpler terms, it means that if a differential form is closed in a region that can be shrunk to a point, then it can be written as the derivative of another form; i.e. if dα = 0 on a simply connected region, we can always find α = dβ; therefore we have d(dβ) = 0, expressed simply as d<sup>2</sup> = 0. This concept is used in mathematical physics, particularly in the context of electromagnetism and [[differential geometry]], where it relates to the fact that the boundary of a boundary is always empty, i.e. if you have a surface (a 2-form) and you take its boundary (a 1-form, a curve), then the boundary of that boundary (a 0-form, a point) is an [[empty set]].

In electromagnetism, magnetic fields can be described using a vector potential, and the Poincaré lemma helps in finding such potentials when the magnetic field is "well-behaved" (i.e., when the magnetic field is not due to a monopole), [[Gauss's law for magnetism]] states that the total magnetic flux through a closed surface is always zero, which implies that magnetic monopoles, if they exist, are not isolated but must be accompanied by other magnetic charges. 

In the language of [[cohomology]], the Poincaré lemma says that the ''k''-th [[de Rham cohomology group]] of a [[contractible space|contractible]] open subset of a manifold ''M'' (e.g., <math>M = \mathbb{R}^n</math>) vanishes for <math>k \ge 1</math>. In particular, it implies that the de Rham complex yields a [[resolution (algebra)|resolution]] of the [[constant sheaf]] <math>\mathbb{R}_M</math> on ''M''. The [[singular cohomology]] of a contractible space vanishes in positive degree, but the Poincaré lemma ''does not follow'' from this, since the fact that the singular cohomology of a manifold can be computed as the de Rham cohomology of it, that is, the [[de Rham theorem]], relies on the Poincaré lemma. It does, however, mean that it is enough to prove the Poincaré lemma for open balls; the version for contractible manifolds then follows from the topological consideration.

The Poincaré lemma is also a special case of the [[homotopy invariance of de Rham cohomology]]; in fact, it is common to establish the lemma by showing the homotopy invariance or at least a version of it.

== Proofs ==
A standard proof of the Poincaré lemma uses the homotopy invariance formula (cf. see the proofs below as well as [[Integration along fibers#Example]]).<ref>{{harvtxt|Lee|2012}}, {{harvtxt|Tu|2011}} and {{harvtxt|Bott|Tu|1982}}.</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Lee|first=John M.|title=Introduction to smooth manifolds|date=2012|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4419-9982-5|edition=2nd|location=New York|oclc=808682771}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Tu|first= Loring W. |title=An introduction to manifolds|title-link=An Introduction to Manifolds|date=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4419-7400-6|edition=2nd|location=New York|oclc=682907530}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Bott|first1=Raoul|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4757-3951-0|title=Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology|last2=Tu|first2=Loring W.|date=1982|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=978-1-4419-2815-3|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|volume=82|location=New York, NY|doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-3951-0}}</ref> The local form of the homotopy operator is described in {{harvtxt|Edelen|2005}} and the connection of the lemma with the [[Maurer–Cartan form|Maurer–Cartan form]] is explained in {{harvtxt|Sharpe|1997}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Edelen|first=Dominic G. B.|title=Applied exterior calculus|date=2005|publisher=Dover Publications|isbn=0-486-43871-6|edition=Rev|location=Mineola, N.Y.|oclc=56347718}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Sharpe|first= R. W.|title=Differential geometry : Cartan's generalization of Klein's Erlangen program|date=1997|publisher=Springer|isbn=0-387-94732-9|location=New York|oclc=34356972}}</ref>

===Direct proof ===
The Poincaré lemma can be proved by means of [[integration along fibers]].<ref name="Conlon">{{harvnb|Conlon|2001|loc=§ 8.3.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.math.brown.edu/reschwar/M114/notes7.pdf | title=The Poincare Lemma | author=Rich Schwartz | website=www.math.brown.edu}}</ref> (This approach is a straightforward generalization of constructing a primitive function by means of integration in calculus.)

We shall prove the lemma for an open subset <math>U \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> that is [[star-shaped]] or a cone over <math>[0, 1]</math>; i.e., if <math>x</math> is in <math>U</math>, then <math>tx</math> is in <math>U</math> for <math>0 \le t \le 1</math>. This case in particular covers the open ball case, since an open ball can be assumed to be centered at the origin [[without loss of generality]].

The trick is to consider differential forms on <math>U \times [0, 1] \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> (we use <math>t</math> for the coordinate on <math>[0, 1]</math>). First define the operator <math>\pi_*</math> (called the [[fiber integration]]) for ''k''-forms on <math>U \times [0, 1]</math> by
:<math>\pi_* \left( \sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_{k-1}} f_i dt \wedge dx^i + \sum_{j_1 < \cdots < j_k} g_j dx^j \right) = \sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_{k-1}} \left( \int_0^1 f_i(\cdot, t) \, dt \right) \, dx^i</math>
where <math>dx^i = dx_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge dx_{i_{k-1}}</math>, <math>f_i = f_{i_1, \dots, i_{k-1}}</math> and similarly for <math>dx^j</math> and <math>g_j</math>. Now, for <math>\alpha = f \, dt \wedge dx^i</math>, since <math>d \alpha = - \sum_l \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_l} dt \wedge dx_l \wedge dx^i</math>, using the [[differentiation under the integral sign]], we have:
:<math>\pi_*(d \alpha) = \alpha_1 - \alpha_0 - d(\pi_* \alpha)</math>
where <math>\alpha_0, \alpha_1</math> denote the restrictions of <math>\alpha</math> to the hyperplanes <math>t = 0, t = 1</math> and they are zero since <math>dt</math> is zero there. If <math>\alpha = g \, dx^j</math>, then a similar computation gives
:<math>\pi_*(d \alpha) = \alpha_1 - \alpha_0 - d(\pi_* \alpha)</math>.
Thus, the above formula holds for any <math>k</math>-form <math>\alpha</math> on <math>U \times [0, 1]</math>. (The formula is a special case of a formula sometimes called the [[relative Stokes formula]].)

Finally, let <math>h(x, t) = tx</math> and then set <math>J = \pi_* \circ h^*</math>. Then, with the notation <math>h_t = h(\cdot, t)</math>, we get: for any <math>k</math>-form <math>\omega</math> on <math>U</math>,
:<math>h_1^* \omega - h_0^* \omega = J d \omega + d J \omega,</math>
the formula known as the homotopy formula. The operator <math>J</math> is called the homotopy operator (also called a [[chain homotopy]]). Now, if <math>\omega</math> is closed, <math>J d \omega = 0</math>. On the other hand, <math>h_1^* \omega = \omega</math> and <math>h_0^* \omega = 0</math>, the latter because there is no nonzero higher form at a point. Hence,
:<math>\omega = d J \omega,</math>
which proves the Poincaré lemma.

The same proof in fact shows the Poincaré lemma for any contractible open subset ''U'' of a manifold. Indeed, given such a ''U'', we have the homotopy <math>h_t</math> with <math>h_1 = </math> the identity and <math>h_0(U) = </math> a point. Approximating such <math>h_t</math>,{{clarify|how exactly|date=November 2024}}, we can assume <math>h_t</math> is in fact smooth. The [[fiber integration]] <math>\pi_*</math> is also defined for <math>\pi : U \times [0, 1] \to U</math>. Hence, the same argument goes through.

=== Proof using Lie derivatives ===
[[Cartan's magic formula]] for [[Lie derivative]]s can be used to give a short proof of the Poincaré lemma. The formula states that the Lie derivative along a [[vector field]] <math>\xi</math> is given as:
<ref>{{harvnb|Warner|1983|pages=69–72}}</ref>
:<math>L_{\xi} = d \, i(\xi) + i(\xi) d</math>
where <math>i(\xi)</math> denotes the [[interior product]]; i.e., <math>i(\xi)\omega = \omega(\xi, \cdot)</math>.

Let <math>f_t : U \to U</math> be a smooth family of smooth maps for some open subset ''U'' of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> such that <math>f_t</math> is defined for ''t'' in some closed interval ''I'' and <math>f_t</math> is a diffeomorphism for ''t'' in the interior of ''I''. Let <math>\xi_t(x)</math> denote the tangent vectors to the curve <math>f_t(x)</math>; i.e., <math>\frac{d}{dt}f_t(x) = \xi_t(f_t(x))</math>. For a fixed ''t'' in the interior of ''I'', let <math>g_s = f_{t + s} \circ f_t^{-1}</math>. Then <math>g_0 = \operatorname{id}, \, \frac{d}{ds}g_s|_{s=0}= \xi_t</math>. Thus, by the definition of a Lie derivative,
:<math>(L_{\xi_t} \omega)(f_t(x)) = \frac{d}{ds} g_s^* \omega(f_t(x))|_{s = 0} = \frac{d}{ds} f_{t+s}^* \omega(x)|_{s = 0} = \frac{d}{dt} f_t^* \omega(x)</math>.
That is,
:<math>\frac{d}{dt} f_t^* \omega = f_t^* L_{\xi_t} \omega.</math>
Assume <math>I = [0, 1]</math>. Then, integrating both sides of the above and then using Cartan's formula and the [[differentiation under the integral sign]], we get: for <math>0 < t_0 < t_1 < 1</math>,
:<math>f_{t_1}^* \omega - f_{t_0}^* \omega = d \int_{t_0}^{t_1} f_t^* i(\xi_t) \omega \, dt + \int_{t_0}^{t_1} f_t^* i(\xi_t) d \omega \, dt</math>
where the integration means the integration of each coefficient in a differential form. Letting <math>t_0, t_1 \to 0, 1</math>, we then have:
:<math>f_1^* \omega - f_0^* \omega = d J \omega + J d \omega</math>
with the notation <math>J \omega = \int_0^1 f_t^* i(\xi_t) \omega \, dt.</math>

Now, assume <math>U</math> is an open ball with center <math>x_0</math>; then we can take <math>f_t(x) = t(x - x_0) + x_0</math>. Then the above formula becomes:
:<math>\omega = d J \omega + J d \omega</math>,
which proves the Poincaré lemma when <math>\omega</math> is closed.

=== Proof in the two-dimensional case===
In two dimensions the Poincaré lemma can be proved directly for closed 1-forms and 2-forms as follows.<ref>{{harvnb|Napier|Ramachandran|2011|pages=443–444}}</ref>

If {{nowrap|1=''ω'' = ''p'' ''dx'' + ''q'' ''dy''}} is a closed 1-form on {{nowrap|(''a'', ''b'') × (''c'', ''d'')}}, then {{nowrap|1=''p''<sub>''y''</sub> = ''q''<sub>''x''</sub>}}. If {{nowrap|1=''ω'' = ''df''}} then {{nowrap|1=''p'' = ''f''<sub>''x''</sub>}} and {{nowrap|1=''q'' = ''f''<sub>''y''</sub>}}. Set

:<math>g(x,y)=\int_a^x p(t,y)\, dt, </math>

so that {{nowrap|1=''g''<sub>''x''</sub> = ''p''}}.  Then {{nowrap|1=''h'' = ''f'' − ''g''}} must satisfy {{nowrap|1=''h''<sub>''x''</sub> = 0}} and {{nowrap|1=''h''<sub>''y''</sub> = ''q'' − ''g''<sub>''y''</sub>}}. The right hand side here is independent of ''x'' since its [[partial derivative]] with respect to ''x'' is <math>q_x-p_y=0</math>. Since <math>q - \partial g/\partial y</math> is independent of ''x'', it is a function of ''y'' only. To find this function, we can evaluate it at any arbitrary value of ''x'', specifically at the boundary <math>x=a</math>:

:<math>h(x,y)=\int_c^y q(a,s)\, ds - g(a,y)=\int_c^y q(a,s)\, ds,</math>

and hence

:<math>f(x,y)=\int_a^x p(t,y)\, dt + \int_c^y q(a,s)\, ds.</math>

Similarly, if {{nowrap|1=Ω = ''r'' ''dx'' ∧ ''dy''}} then {{nowrap|1=Ω = ''d''(''a'' ''dx'' + ''b'' ''dy'')}} with {{nowrap|1=''b''<sub>''x''</sub> − ''a''<sub>''y''</sub> = ''r''}}. Thus a solution is given by {{nowrap|1=''a'' = 0}} and

:<math>b(x,y)=\int_a^x r(t,y) \, dt. </math>

=== Inductive proof ===
It is also possible to give an inductive proof of Poincaré's lemma which does not use homotopical arguments. Let <math>X_m:=I^m</math>, where <math>I = (-1, 1)</math>, be an m dimensional open coordinate cube. For each <math>n \le m</math> the projection <math>\pi_{m,n}:X_m\rightarrow X_n</math> which deletes the last m-n coordinates of a point is a fibration and therefore the pullback map <math>\pi^\ast_{m,n}:\Omega^\bullet(X_n)\rightarrow\Omega^\bullet(X_m)</math> is a monomorphism. We may thus consider any differential k-form which is defined on <math>X_n</math> to be also defined on <math>X_m</math> with no additional notation. Conversely, a k-form <math>\omega\in\Omega^k(X_m)</math> descends to a (necessarily unique) k-form on <math>X_n</math> [[if and only if]] its expression with respect to the standard coordinates is

<math display="inline">\omega = \sum_{0\le i_1<\dots<i_k\le n}\omega_{i_1...i_k}(x^1,\dots,x^n)dx^{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx^{i_k}</math>,

or in other words, its coefficients are functions of the variables <math>x^1,\dots,x^n</math> only, and differentials of only the latter variables are involved.

For a differential ''k''-form <math>\omega\in\Omega^k(X_m)</math>, let its ''codegree'' be the integer ''m-k''. The induction is performed over the codegree of the form. Since we are working over a coordinate domain, partial derivatives and also integrals with respect to the coordinates can be applied to a form itself, by applying them to the coefficients of the form with respect to the [[canonical coordinates]].

First let <math>\omega\in\Omega^m(X_m)</math>, i.e. the codegree is 0. It can be written as <math display="block">\omega = dx^m\wedge \omega_0,\quad \omega_0 = f(x^1,\dots,x^m)dx^1\wedge\dots\wedge dx^{m-1}</math>so if we define <math>\theta\in \Omega^{m-1}(X_m)</math> by <math>\theta = \int_0^{x_m}\omega_0(x^1,\dots,x^{m-1},s)\,ds</math>, we have<math display="block">d\theta = dx^m\wedge \partial_m\theta =dx^m\wedge\omega_0 = \omega</math>hence, <math>\theta</math> is a primitive of <math>\omega</math>.

Let now <math>\omega\in\Omega^k(X_m)</math>, where <math>0<k<m</math>, i.e. <math>\omega</math> has codegree ''m-k'', and let us suppose that whenever a closed form has codegree less than ''m-k'', the form is exact. The form <math>\omega</math> can be decomposed as<math display="block">\omega = dx^m\wedge\omega_0 + \omega_1</math>where neither <math>\omega_0</math> nor <math>\omega_1</math> contain any factor of <math>dx^m</math>. Define <math>\lambda:=\int_0^{x_m}\omega_0(x^1,\dots,x^{m-1},s)\,ds</math>, then <math>d\lambda = dx^m\wedge\omega_0 + \lambda_1</math>, where <math>\lambda_1</math> does not contain any factor of <math>dx^m</math>, hence, defining <math>\omega^\prime:=\omega-d\lambda=\omega_1 -\lambda_1</math>, this form is also closed, but does not involve any factor of <math>dx^m</math>. Since this form is closed, we have<math display="block">0=d\omega^\prime = dx^m\wedge\partial_m\omega^\prime + \omega^{\prime\prime}</math>where the last term does not contain a factor of <math>dx^m</math>. Due to [[linear independence]] of the coordinate differentials, this equation implies that<math display="block">\omega^\prime=\sum_{1\le i_1<\dots<i_k\le m-1}\omega_{i_1...i_k}(x^1,\dots,x^{m-1})dx^{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx^{i_k}</math>i.e. the form <math>\omega^\prime</math> is a differential form in the variables <math>x^1,\dots,x^{m-1}</math> only, hence it descends to an element of <math>\Omega^{k}(X_{m-1})</math>, and its codegree is thus ''m-k-1''. The induction hypothesis applies, thus <math>\omega^\prime = d\theta^{\prime}</math> for some <math>\theta^{\prime}\in\Omega^{k-1}(X_{m-1})\subseteq\Omega^{k-1}(X_m)</math>, therefore<math display="block">\omega = d\theta,\quad \theta = \theta^\prime + \lambda</math>concluding the proof for a coordinate cube. In any manifold, every point has a neighborhood which is diffeomorphic to a coordinate cube, the proof also implies that on a manifold any closed ''k''-form (for <math>0<k\le m=\dim M</math>) is locally exact.

== Implication for de Rham cohomology ==
By definition, the ''k''-th [[de Rham cohomology]] group <math>\operatorname{H}_{dR}^k(U)</math> of an open subset ''U'' of a manifold ''M'' is defined as the quotient [[vector space]]
:<math>\operatorname{H}_{dR}^k(U) = \{ \textrm{ closed } \, k\text{-forms} \, \textrm { on } \, U \}/\{ \textrm{ exact } \, k\text{-forms} \, \textrm { on } \, U \}.</math>
Hence, the conclusion of the Poincaré lemma is precisely that if <math>U</math> is an open ball, then <math>\operatorname{H}_{dR}^k(U) = 0</math> for <math>k \ge 1</math>. Now, differential forms determine a [[cochain complex]] called the de Rham complex:
:<math>\Omega^* : 0 \to \Omega^0 \overset{d^0}\to \Omega^1 \overset{d^1}\to \cdots \to \Omega^n \to 0</math>
where ''n'' = the dimension of ''M'' and <math>\Omega^k</math> denotes the sheaf of differential ''k''-forms; i.e., <math>\Omega^k(U)</math> consists of ''k''-forms on ''U'' for each open subset ''U'' of ''M''. It then gives rise to the complex (the augmented complex)
:<math>0 \to \mathbb{R}_M \overset{\epsilon}\to \Omega^0 \overset{d^0}\to \Omega^1 \overset{d^1}\to \cdots \to \Omega^n \to 0</math>
where <math>\mathbb{R}_M</math> is the constant sheaf with values in <math>\mathbb{R}</math>; i.e., it is the sheaf of locally constant real-valued functions and <math>\epsilon</math> the inclusion.

The kernel of <math>d^0</math> is <math>\mathbb{R}_M</math>, since the smooth functions with zero derivatives are locally constant. Also, a sequence of sheaves is exact if and only if it is so locally.  The Poincaré lemma thus says the rest of the sequence is exact too (since a manifold is locally diffeomorphic to an open subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and then each point has an open ball as a neighborhood). In the language of [[homological algebra]], it means that the de Rham complex determines a [[resolution (algebra)|resolution]] of the constant sheaf <math>\mathbb{R}_M</math>. This then implies the [[de Rham theorem]]; i.e., the de Rham cohomology of a manifold coincides with the singular cohomology of it (in short, because the singular cohomology can be viewed as a [[sheaf cohomology]].)

Once one knows the de Rham theorem, the conclusion of the Poincaré lemma can then be obtained purely topologically. For example, it implies a version of the Poincaré lemma for contractible or [[simply connected]] open sets (see [[#Simply_connected_case|§Simply connected case]]).

== Simply connected case ==
Especially in [[calculus]], the Poincaré lemma is stated for a simply connected open subset <math>U \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math>. In that case, the lemma says that each closed 1-form on ''U'' is exact. This version can be seen using [[algebraic topology]] as follows. The [[rational Hurewicz theorem]] (or rather the real analog of that) says that <math>\operatorname{H}_1(U; \mathbb{R}) = 0</math> since ''U'' is simply connected. Since <math>\mathbb{R}</math> is a field, the ''k''-th cohomology <math>\operatorname{H}^k(U; \mathbb{R})</math> is the dual vector space of the ''k''-th homology <math>\operatorname{H}_k(U; \mathbb{R})</math>. In particular, <math>\operatorname{H}^1(U; \mathbb{R}) = 0.</math> By the de Rham theorem (which follows from the Poincaré lemma for open balls), <math>\operatorname{H}^1(U; \mathbb{R})</math> is the same as the first de Rham cohomology group (see [[#Implication to de Rham cohomology|§Implication to de Rham cohomology]]). Hence, each closed 1-form on ''U'' is exact.

== Poincaré lemma with compact support ==
There is a version of Poincaré lemma for compactly supported differential forms:<ref>{{harvnb|Conlon|2001|loc=Corollary 8.3.17.}}</ref>

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma|math_statement=If <math>\omega</math> is a closed <math>p</math>-form with compact support on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> and if <math>p < n</math>, then there is a compactly supported <math>(p-1)</math>-form <math>\psi</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> such that <math>d \psi = \omega</math>.}}

The usual proof in the non-compact case does not go through since the homotopy ''h'' is not proper. Thus, somehow a different argument is needed for the compact case.

==Complex-geometry analog==
On [[complex manifold]]s, the use of the [[Dolbeault operator]]s <math>\partial</math> and <math>\bar \partial</math> for [[complex differential form]]s, which refine the [[exterior derivative]] by the formula <math>d=\partial + \bar \partial</math>, lead to the notion of <math>\bar \partial</math>-closed and <math>\bar \partial</math>-exact differential forms. The local exactness result for such closed forms is known as the [[Dolbeault-Grothendieck lemma|Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma]] (or <math>\bar \partial</math>-Poincaré lemma); cf. {{section link||On polynomial differential forms}}. Importantly, the geometry of the domain on which a <math>\bar \partial</math>-closed differential form is <math>\bar \partial</math>-exact is more restricted than for the Poincaré lemma, since the proof of the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma holds on a polydisk (a product of disks in the complex plane, on which the multidimensional [[Cauchy's integral formula]] may be applied) and there exist counterexamples to the lemma even on contractible domains.<ref group="Note">For counterexamples on contractible domains which have non-vanishing first Dolbeault cohomology see {{Cite web | url=https://mathoverflow.net/a/59554 | title=∂∂ lemma for contractible domains | website=mathoverflow.net}}</ref> The <math>\bar \partial</math>-Poincaré lemma holds in more generality for [[pseudoconvex domain]]s.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-48016-4_7|chapter=On the Cohomology Structure of Stein Manifolds |title=Proceedings of the Conference on Complex Analysis |year=1965 |last1=Aeppli |first1=A. |pages=58–70 |isbn=978-3-642-48018-8 }}</ref>

Using both the Poincaré lemma and the <math>\bar \partial</math>-Poincaré lemma, a refined [[Local ddbar lemma|local <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-Poincaré lemma]] can be proven, which is valid on domains upon which both the aforementioned lemmas are applicable. This lemma states that <math>d</math>-closed complex differential forms are actually locally <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-exact (rather than just <math>d</math> or <math>\bar \partial</math>-exact, as implied by the above lemmas).

== Relative Poincaré lemma ==
The '''relative Poincaré lemma''' generalizes Poincaré lemma from a point to a submanifold (or some more general [[locally closed subset]]). It states: let ''V'' be a submanifold of a manifold ''M'' and ''U'' a [[tubular neighborhood]] of ''V''. If <math>\sigma</math> is a closed ''k''-form on ''U'', ''k'' ≥ 1, that vanishes on ''V'', then there exists a (''k''-1)-form <math>\eta</math> on ''U'' such that <math>d \eta = \sigma</math> and <math>\eta</math> vanishes on ''V''.<ref>{{cite journal |s2cid=51762845 |doi=10.1215/IJM/1258131054 |title=Relative Poincaré lemma, contractibility, quasi-homogeneity and vector fields tangent to a singular variety § 2. Relative Poincare lemma and contractibility|year=2004 |last1=Domitrz |first1=W. |last2=Janeczko |first2=S. |last3=Zhitomirskii |first3=M. |journal=Illinois Journal of Mathematics |volume=48 |issue=3 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The relative Poincaré lemma can be proved in the same way the original Poincaré lemma is proved. Indeed, since ''U'' is a tubular neighborhood, there is a smooth strong deformation retract from ''U'' to ''V''; i.e., there is a smooth homotopy <math>h_t : U \to U</math> from the projection <math>U \to V</math> to the identity such that <math>h_t</math> is the identity on ''V''. Then we have the homotopy formula on ''U'':
:<math>h_1^* - h_0^* = d J + J d</math>
where <math>J</math> is the homotopy operator given by either [[Lie derivative]]s or [[integration along fibers]]. Now, <math>h_0 (U) \subset V</math> and so <math>h_0^* \sigma = 0</math>. Since <math>d \sigma = 0</math> and <math>h_1^* \sigma = \sigma</math>, we get <math>\sigma = d J \sigma</math>; take <math>\eta = J \sigma</math>. That <math>\eta</math> vanishes on ''V'' follows from the definition of ''J'' and the fact <math>h_t(V) \subset V</math>. (So the proof actually goes through if ''U'' is not a tubular neighborhood but if ''U'' deformation-retracts to ''V'' with homotopy relative to ''V''.) <math>\square</math>

== On polynomial differential forms ==
In characteristic zero, the following Poincaré lemma holds for [[polynomial differential form]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1975|loc=Ch. II., Proposition 7.1.}}</ref>

Let ''k'' be a field of characteristic zero, <math>R = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]</math> the [[polynomial ring]] and <math>\Omega^1</math> the vector space with a basis written as <math>dx_1, \dots, d x_n</math>. Then let <math>\Omega^p = \wedge^p \Omega^1</math> be the ''p''-th exterior power of <math>\Omega^1</math> over <math>R</math>. Then the sequence of vector spaces
:<math>0 \to k \to \Omega^0 \overset{d}\to \Omega^1 \overset{d}\to \cdots \to 0</math>
is exact, where the differential <math>d</math> is defined by the usual way; i.e., the linearity and
:<math>d (f \, d x_{i_i} \wedge \cdots \wedge d x_{i_p}) = \sum_j \frac{\partial f}{d x_j} dx_j \wedge d x_{i_i} \wedge \cdots \wedge d x_{i_p}.</math>

This version of the lemma is seen by a calculus-like argument. First note that <math>\ker(d : R \to \Omega^1) = k</math>, clearly. Thus, we only need to check the exactness at <math>p > 0</math>. Let <math>\omega</math> be a <math>p</math>-form. Then we write
:<math>\omega = \omega_0 \wedge dx_1 + \omega_1</math>
where the <math>\omega_i</math>'s do not involve <math>dx_1</math>. Define the integration in <math>x_1</math> by the linearity and 
:<math>\int x_1^r \, dx_1 = \frac{x_1^{r+1}}{r+1},</math>
which is well-defined by the char zero assumption. Then let
:<math>\eta = \int \omega_0 \, dx_1</math>
where the integration is applied to each coefficient in <math>\omega_0</math>. Clearly, the [[fundamental theorem of calculus]] holds in our formal setup and thus we get:
:<math>d \eta = \omega_0 \wedge \, dx_1 + \sigma</math>
where <math>\sigma</math> does not involve <math>dx_1</math>. Hence, <math>\omega - d \eta</math> ''does not involve <math>dx_1</math>.'' Replacing <math>\omega</math> by <math>\omega - d \eta</math>, we can thus assume <math>\omega</math> does not involve <math>dx_1</math>. From the assumption <math>d \omega = 0</math>, it easily follows that each coefficient in <math>\omega</math> is independent of <math>x_1</math>; i.e., <math>\omega</math> is a polynomial differential form in the variables <math>x_2, \dots, x_n</math>. Hence, we are done by induction. <math>\square</math>

'''Remark:''' With the same proof, the same results hold when <math>R = k[\![x_1, \dots, x_n]\!]</math> is the ring of [[formal power series]] or the ring of germs of [[holomorphic functions]].<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1975|loc=Ch. II., Remark after Proposition 7.1.}}</ref> A suitably modified proof also shows the <math>\bar \partial</math>-Poincaré lemma; namely, the use of the fundamental theorem of calculus is replaced by [[Cauchy's integral formula]].<ref>Theorem 2.3.3. in {{Citation |last= Hörmander |first =Lars |authorlink =Lars Hörmander |date=1990 |orig-year=1966 |title=An Introduction to Complex Analysis in Several Variables |edition=3rd |publisher=North Holland |isbn=978-1-493-30273-4 |url={{Google books|MaM7AAAAQBAJ|An Introduction to Complex Analysis in Several Variables|plainurl=yes}}}}</ref>

== On singular spaces ==
The Poincaré lemma generally fails for singular spaces. For example, if one considers ''algebraic'' differential forms on a complex [[algebraic variety]] (in the Zariski topology), the lemma is not true for those differential forms.<ref>{{harvnb|Illusie|2012|loc=§ 1.}}</ref> One way to resolve this is to use [[formal function|formal forms]] and the resulting [[algebraic de Rham cohomology]] can compute a singular cohomology.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1975|loc=Ch. IV., Theorem 1.1.}}</ref>

However, the variants of the lemma still likely hold for some singular spaces (precise formulation and proof depend on the definitions of such spaces and non-smooth differential forms on them). For example, [[Maxim Kontsevich|Kontsevich]] and [[Yan Soibelman|Soibelman]] claim the lemma holds for certain variants of different forms (called PA forms) on their [[piecewise algebraic space]]s.<ref>{{cite book | title=Conférence Moshé Flato 1999: Quantization, Deformations, and Symmetries I |chapter=Deformations of algebras over operads and Deligne's conjecture| isbn=9780792365402 | last1=Kontsevich | first1=Maxim | last2=Soibelman | first2=Yan | year=2000|arxiv=math/0001151|pages=255–307}}</ref>

The [[homotopy invariance]] fails for [[intersection cohomology]]; in particular, the Poincaré lemma fails for such cohomology.
